title: Setting out
hook: Nanak leaves home for years of travel on foot, with Mardana beside him

segments.voice: Yesterday, the rebab, and Mardana playing so Nanak could sing. Your line was one plays, one sings. Who did you notice working at the side of the stage? Day thirty-two.

A daily map can shrink to a few streets: the grocery store, the office, a couple of friends' houses, and the route between them, walked so often it could be drawn with eyes shut. Guru Nanak had a good job in Sultanpur, a wife, two young sons, a sister nearby who loved him. And then, some time after the river, he left it all and started walking. Not for a weekend. For years. On foot, with Mardana and the rebab beside him, sleeping where they were offered a floor and eating what they were given. From here the story changes shape. It stops being one village and becomes a road. Today, the word for that road.
screen: `A JOB, A FAMILY, A TOWN.` → `THEN HE STARTED WALKING.` → `FOR YEARS, ON FOOT.`

segments.voice: Sikhs call these journeys the udasis. Tradition counts four great ones, sometimes five, spread over many years. One went east, toward Bengal and Assam. One went south, as far as Sri Lanka, tradition says. One north, into the Himalayas. One west, as far as Mecca and Baghdad. Nobody has a travel log. What we have are the janamsakhis, life stories written down generations later, and they don't always agree on the order or the route. So the dates and the map are tradition, and Sikh historians still argue over them. Now the word itself. Udasi comes from a word that can mean detachment, even sadness, the feeling of someone who has stepped back from the world. In Nanak's time it could describe a renunciate, a wandering holy man who gave up home for good. Here's the surprise. Nanak walked like a renunciate, but he didn't preach renunciation. He came home between journeys. His hymns don't ask people to abandon their families. His travels were for going out to people, not away from them. He went to the pilgrimage towns, the Muslim shrines, the mountain hermitages and the markets, and he talked with whoever was there: priests, Sufis, yogis, carpenters, thieves. And stop after stop becomes a story, a short, sharp scene that Sikh children grow up hearing. Over the next week or so we'll take them one at a time, as shorts. Today is the day the car pulls out of the driveway. Everything he'd said at home, there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim, he now takes out on the road, to see if it holds up.
screen: `FOUR JOURNEYS, TRADITION SAYS.` · `THE MAP IS TRADITION, NOT A LOG.` · `UDASI — STEPPING BACK.` · `NOT AWAY FROM PEOPLE. OUT TO THEM.` · then, large: `GO AND SEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk somewhere new today. It doesn't have to be far. A street you've never turned down. The other staircase at work. The far end of the park. For now, settle and plan it. Picture the door you'll walk out of. Picture the turn you don't usually take. Then, when you get there, look the way a traveler looks, as if you might have to describe it to someone back home. The bell holds the time.
Udasi. The name for Guru Nanak's long journeys on foot, from a word for detachment, stepping back. Today's word.
Your line: go and see. Today, take the new route, and talk to one person there you wouldn't normally talk to. Day thirty-two.

howItsDone: Sikhs remember Guru Nanak's udasis through the sakhis, short stories of each stop, told at home, in gurdwaras and in children's classes; many gurdwaras across South Asia stand at places tradition links to his travels.

original.note: Gurmukhi: udasi, from a word for detachment or sadness; for Sikhs, the name of Guru Nanak's journeys.

trapdoor: what you thought: Guru Nanak went traveling.
what it means: udasi, years of journeys on foot to meet people of every faith, while never preaching that anyone should leave home.
what a scholar hears: a word used for renunciates, borrowed for journeys that were not renunciation; routes and dates come from later janamsakhis that disagree.

notes: Number of udasis (four, sometimes five), directions and 'about twenty years' follow common tradition; dates vary widely between sources. Confirm.
Sri Lanka, Mecca and Baghdad as destinations are traditional; historians debate some of them. Framed as 'tradition says'. Confirm.
Etymology of udasi (detachment, sadness; used of renunciates, and later the name of the Udasi order) should be checked.
Nanak's family at departure (wife Mata Sulakhni, sons Sri Chand and Lakhmi Das) is alluded to, not named; confirm.
Editor review: hook no longer tells the listener 'most of us'; cut the unsourced 'something like twenty years'; 'he never told people' became what his hymns do not ask; 'almost every stop' softened.
